Detective: it spots the forced entry
Corrective: it repairs the door
decouverte.answer: Detective: it spots the forced entry
decouverte.explanation: The alarm blocks nobody. It raises the alert. The first answer is tempting because noise feels like a protection, but noise stops nothing.

decouverte.titre: The day of a computer attack
decouverte.texte: A firewall blocks most attacks: it is preventative. An IDS is a system that watches the network and raises an alert. It reports the attacks that get through: it is detective. The patch that closes the weakness is corrective. The backup gets the site running again: it is recovery. Guards at the entrance are deterrent.

cards.question: Official definition: “preventative controls”
cards.answer: Preventative: These are the first-line controls that are designed to keep adverse security events from occurring.
cards.explanation: Preventative controls act first. They try to stop a bad event before it happens.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Applicable Types of Controls”. Examples from the manual: input checking in software, firewalls, backups and awareness training.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “preventative controls”?
options: Preventative: These are the first-line controls that are designed to identify adverse security events while occurring.
Preventative: These are the first-line controls that are designed to repair adverse security events after occurring.
Preventative: These are the last-line controls that are designed to keep adverse security events from occurring.
Preventative: These are the first-line controls that are designed to keep adverse security events from occurring.
options_why: Identifying an event is the job of detective controls.
Repairing damage after an event is the job of corrective controls.
Preventative controls are the first line, not the last.
cards.answer: Preventative: These are the first-line controls that are designed to keep adverse security events from occurring.
cards.explanation: Think of the lock on the house: the first line, before the event.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “preventative controls” from memory.
cards.answer: Preventative: These are the first-line controls that are designed to keep adverse security events from occurring.
cards.explanation: Think of the lock on the house: the first line, before the event.

cards.question: Official definition: “detective controls”
cards.answer: Detective: These controls are designed to identify a negative security event while it is in progress or soon after it occurs.
cards.explanation: Detective controls spot a bad event while it happens or just after. An alarm is one example.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Applicable Types of Controls”. Examples from the manual: security audits, door alarms and IDSs.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “detective controls”?
options: Detective: These controls are designed to prevent a negative security event while it is in progress or soon after it occurs.
Detective: These controls are designed to identify a negative security event only after it is fully over.
Detective: These controls are designed to repair a negative security event while it is in progress or soon after it occurs.
Detective: These controls are designed to identify a negative security event while it is in progress or soon after it occurs.
options_why: Preventing happens before the event. That is the job of preventative controls.
Detective controls work while the event happens or soon after, not only when it is over.
Repairing damage is the job of corrective controls.
cards.answer: Detective: These controls are designed to identify a negative security event while it is in progress or soon after it occurs.
cards.explanation: Think of the alarm: it spots the event during it or just after.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “detective controls” from memory.
cards.answer: Detective: These controls are designed to identify a negative security event while it is in progress or soon after it occurs.
cards.explanation: Think of the alarm: it spots the event during it or just after.

cards.question: Official definition: “corrective controls”
cards.answer: Corrective: These controls are designed to minimize and repair damages following an adverse security event; they are typically put in place after a detective control identifies a problem.
cards.explanation: Corrective controls limit the damage and repair it. They usually come after a detective control finds the problem.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Applicable Types of Controls”. Examples from the manual: software patches, changes to configuration files and new policies that target the cause.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “corrective controls”?
options: Corrective: These controls are designed to minimize and repair damages following an adverse security event; they are typically put in place before a detective control identifies a problem.
Corrective: These controls are designed to minimize and repair damages following an adverse security event; they are typically put in place after a detective control identifies a problem.
Corrective: These controls are designed to minimize and repair damages following an adverse security event; they are typically put in place after a preventative control identifies a problem.
Corrective: These controls are designed to identify and report damages following an adverse security event; they are typically put in place after a detective control identifies a problem.
options_why: Corrective controls come after the detective control has found the problem.
Preventative controls do not identify problems. Detective controls do.
Identify and report is the job of detective controls. Corrective controls minimize and repair.
cards.answer: Corrective: These controls are designed to minimize and repair damages following an adverse security event; they are typically put in place after a detective control identifies a problem.
cards.explanation: Think of the window repaired after the alarm: limit and repair, after the problem was found.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “corrective controls” from memory.
cards.answer: Corrective: These controls are designed to minimize and repair damages following an adverse security event; they are typically put in place after a detective control identifies a problem.
cards.explanation: Think of the window repaired after the alarm: limit and repair, after the problem was found.

cards.question: Official definition: “recovery controls”
cards.answer: Recovery: These countermeasures are designed to complement corrective controls, with the intent to get a system back to normal as quickly as possible.
cards.explanation: Recovery controls get a system running again as fast as possible. Backups and backup sites are examples.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Applicable Types of Controls”. Examples from the manual: system and data backups and disaster recovery sites.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “recovery controls” from memory.
cards.answer: Recovery: These countermeasures are designed to complement corrective controls, with the intent to get a system back to normal as quickly as possible.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: they complement corrective controls, get the system back to normal, and do it fast.

cards.question: Official definition: “deterrent controls”
cards.answer: Deterrent: These controls are designed to discourage attackers by making them think twice about their malicious intents.
cards.explanation: Deterrent controls work on the mind of the attacker. The attacker gives up before trying.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Applicable Types of Controls”. Examples from the manual: wire fences, security guards and guard dogs.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “deterrent controls” from memory.
cards.answer: Deterrent: These controls are designed to discourage attackers by making them think twice about their malicious intents.
cards.explanation: Discourage attackers, make them think twice, about their bad plans.

cards.question: A firewall blocks an attack before it gets in. Which type of control is it?
options: Detective
Corrective
Preventative
Deterrent
options_why: A detective control spots an event. This one blocks it.
A corrective control repairs damage after an event.
A deterrent control works on the mind of the attacker. A firewall blocks traffic.
cards.answer: Preventative
cards.explanation: It acts before the incident, by blocking. That is a preventative control.

cards.question: A door alarm rings when someone forces the entrance. Which type of control is it?
options: Detective
Preventative
Corrective
Recovery
options_why: The alarm blocks nobody. It only raises the alert.
The alarm does not repair anything.
The alarm does not bring any system back to normal.
cards.answer: Detective
cards.explanation: The alarm spots the event while it happens. Door alarms are the manual's example of a detective control.

cards.question: A software patch closes a weakness after an attack. Which type of control is it?
options: Preventative
Corrective
Detective
Deterrent
options_why: A patch is put in place after a problem was found, to repair its cause.
A patch does not spot anything. It repairs.
A patch does not discourage anyone.
cards.answer: Corrective
cards.explanation: Patches repair the cause of an incident. The manual lists them as corrective controls.

cards.question: After a server crash, a company must get its service back as fast as possible. Which control is BEST suited?
options: A backup site (recovery)
A security audit (detective)
A guard dog (deterrent)
Input checking in the software (preventative)
options_why: An audit finds problems. It does not bring a service back.
A guard dog scares intruders. It does not restore a server.
Input checking acts before an incident, not after a crash.
cards.answer: A backup site (recovery)
cards.explanation: Recovery controls get a system back to normal as quickly as possible.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Applicable Types of Controls”. The manual lists backups in both the preventative and the recovery examples.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a detective control?
options: A security audit
A door alarm
An IDS that raises an alert
A software patch
options_why: An audit looks for problems. It is detective.
An alarm spots a break-in. It is detective.
An IDS watches the network and reports attacks. It is detective.
cards.answer: A software patch
cards.explanation: A patch repairs a weakness. That is a corrective control.

cards.question: Which type of control acts FIRST in time, before an incident happens?
options: Detective
Corrective
Preventative
Recovery
options_why: Detective controls act during or just after an event.
Corrective controls act after the problem was found.
Recovery controls act after the damage is done.
cards.answer: Preventative
cards.explanation: Preventative controls are the first-line controls.

cards.question: Wire fences and guard dogs are meant to make attackers think twice. Which type of control MOST fits them?
options: Preventative
Detective
Deterrent
Corrective
options_why: A fence can block, but the manual lists it as a deterrent that works on the mind of the attacker.
A fence does not spot an event.
A fence does not repair anything.
cards.answer: Deterrent
cards.explanation: Deterrent controls discourage attackers before they try.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Applicable Types of Controls”.

cards.question: A shop installs an alarm that rings when the back door is forced. Later, the manager replaces the damaged door. Which two types do we see, in order?
options: Preventative, then detective
Corrective, then deterrent
Deterrent, then recovery
Detective, then corrective
options_why: The alarm blocks nothing, so it is not preventative.
The alarm does not repair. The new door does not scare anyone in advance.
The alarm spots an event. A new door repairs damage.
cards.answer: Detective, then corrective
cards.explanation: The alarm spots the break-in. Replacing the door repairs the damage.

cards.question: A team applies a patch that removes the cause of an outage. Another team restores the data from backups. Which statement is BEST?
options: The patch is corrective. The restore is recovery
The patch is recovery. The restore is corrective
Both actions are corrective
Both actions are preventative
options_why: This is the wrong way round.
The restore aims to bring the system back to normal fast. That is recovery.
Both happen after the incident.
cards.answer: The patch is corrective. The restore is recovery
cards.explanation: Corrective controls repair the damage and the cause. Recovery controls bring the system back fast.

cards.question: Why does a company need a detective control on top of a preventative control?
options: Detective controls stop attacks before they start, so nothing gets through
No barrier stops everything, so attacks that get through must be seen
Preventative controls can be removed once detective ones exist
Auditors only accept detective controls
options_why: Stopping attacks is the job of preventative controls.
You still need both.
Auditors do not choose the type of control.
cards.answer: No barrier stops everything, so attacks that get through must be seen
cards.explanation: If an attack gets through, spotting it fast limits the damage.

cards.question: Which statement about the types of controls is correct?
options: Each countermeasure fits exactly one type
One countermeasure, such as a guard, can fit several types
Types apply only to technology, such as firewalls and software
Only preventative controls count as real controls
options_why: The manual says some countermeasures fit into several categories.
Guards, fences and rules are also controls.
All five types are real controls.
cards.answer: One countermeasure, such as a guard, can fit several types
cards.explanation: A guard can deter, spot and react. The types describe a role.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Applicable Types of Controls”.

cards.question: What is a recovery control for?
cards.answer: To get a system back to normal as quickly as possible. Examples are backups and backup sites.
cards.explanation: Think of getting the website running again.

cards.question: Name two examples of preventative controls.
cards.answer: For example: a firewall, input checking in software, or security awareness training.
cards.explanation: They act before the event.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Applicable Types of Controls”.

cards.question: What is the difference between corrective and recovery controls?
cards.answer: Corrective controls repair the damage and the cause. Recovery controls bring the system back to normal fast.
cards.explanation: Fix the cause, then get running again.

cards.question: What do deterrent controls work on?
cards.answer: The mind of the attacker. They make the attacker think twice and give up.
cards.explanation: A fence or a guard dog is a deterrent.

paragraphes: Your bike is worth $300. A seller offers you a golden helmet for $5,000, “the safest in the world”. You do not buy it.
You also do not choose a helmet so heavy that you leave it at home.
To choose a protection, you ask three questions. Does it really protect? Does it cost less than the loss? Is it easy to use?

decouverte.comme: A helmet must protect against the right danger. It must cost less than the damage. It must be comfortable enough that you really wear it.
decouverte.enVrai: Security-effectiveness: does the measure deal well with the risk you target? Cost-effectiveness: does it cost less than the loss it prevents? Operational impact: does it get in the way of work so much that nobody uses it?

decouverte.question: A server may lose power for hours. The company encrypts all its files. Is this the right measure?
options: Yes: encryption protects against everything
No: encryption does not fix an access problem
Yes, but only at night
decouverte.answer: No: encryption does not fix an access problem
decouverte.explanation: Encryption protects secrecy. It does not keep files available. Against a power failure, a backup is more effective. The manual gives this example.

decouverte.texte: ALE means annual loss expectancy: the money you expect to lose in one year because of a risk. Thefts cost $18,000 a year, so the ALE is $18,000. An anti-theft system costs $5,000 a year and brings the ALE down to $6,000. Total with the system: 6,000 + 5,000 = $11,000. That is less than $18,000, so the system saves $7,000 a year.

decouverte.titre: The tool that is too hard
decouverte.texte: A company forces everyone to use a very hard email encryption tool. Employees find it a pain. Some of them send sensitive emails without encryption. The protection exists, but the risk has gone up.

cards.question: Official definition: “cost-effective” (a countermeasure worth its price)
cards.answer: A countermeasure can be considered cost-effective if the annual loss expectancy (ALE) with the countermeasure plus the cost of countermeasure is less than ALE without the countermeasure.
cards.explanation: A countermeasure is worth its price when the ALE with it, plus its cost, is smaller than the ALE without it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Cost-Effectiveness”. ALE means annual loss expectancy.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “cost-effective”?
options: A countermeasure can be considered cost-effective if the annual loss expectancy (ALE) with the countermeasure plus the cost of countermeasure is more than ALE without the countermeasure.
A countermeasure can be considered cost-effective if the annual loss expectancy (ALE) with the countermeasure is less than the cost of countermeasure.
A countermeasure can be considered cost-effective if the annual loss expectancy (ALE) with the countermeasure minus the cost of countermeasure is less than ALE without the countermeasure.
A countermeasure can be considered cost-effective if the annual loss expectancy (ALE) with the countermeasure plus the cost of countermeasure is less than ALE without the countermeasure.
options_why: If the total is more, the measure costs more than it saves.
The test compares two totals: ALE with the measure plus its cost, against the ALE without it.
The cost is added to the ALE, not taken away.
cards.answer: A countermeasure can be considered cost-effective if the annual loss expectancy (ALE) with the countermeasure plus the cost of countermeasure is less than ALE without the countermeasure.
cards.explanation: ALE with the measure, plus its cost, must stay smaller than the ALE without the measure.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “cost-effective” from memory.
cards.answer: A countermeasure can be considered cost-effective if the annual loss expectancy (ALE) with the countermeasure plus the cost of countermeasure is less than ALE without the countermeasure.
cards.explanation: ALE with the measure, plus its cost, must stay smaller than the ALE without the measure.

cards.question: Official definition: the factors to consider when choosing a countermeasure
cards.answer: When selecting countermeasures, you must consider factors such as security-effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and operational impact.
cards.explanation: Check three things before you choose: does it protect, is it worth its price, and does it block the work?
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Countermeasure Selection and Implementation”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official one about “the factors for choosing a countermeasure”?
options: When selecting countermeasures, you must consider factors such as security-effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and operational impact.
When selecting countermeasures, you must consider factors such as security-effectiveness, popularity, and operational impact.
When selecting countermeasures, you must consider factors such as security-effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and the opinion of vendors.
When selecting countermeasures, you should consider factors such as cost-effectiveness and operational impact only.
options_why: Popularity is not one of the factors. The second factor is cost-effectiveness.
The third factor is operational impact, not the opinion of vendors.
Security-effectiveness is the first factor. A cheap measure that does not protect is useless.
cards.answer: When selecting countermeasures, you must consider factors such as security-effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and operational impact.
cards.explanation: Three factors: security-effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and operational impact.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about “the factors for choosing a countermeasure” from memory.
cards.answer: When selecting countermeasures, you must consider factors such as security-effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and operational impact.
cards.explanation: Three factors: security-effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and operational impact.

cards.question: Official definition: calculating “cost-effectiveness”
cards.answer: Cost-effectiveness can be calculated by performing a cost-benefit analysis that compares the cost of a countermeasure (or multiple countermeasures) to the costs that would be realized by a compromise of the risks that the countermeasures are intended to mitigate.
cards.explanation: To check cost-effectiveness, you do a cost-benefit analysis. You compare what the protection costs with what the problem would cost.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Cost-Effectiveness”.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about “calculating cost-effectiveness” from memory.
cards.answer: Cost-effectiveness can be calculated by performing a cost-benefit analysis that compares the cost of a countermeasure (or multiple countermeasures) to the costs that would be realized by a compromise of the risks that the countermeasures are intended to mitigate.
cards.explanation: A cost-benefit analysis: the cost of the measure against the costs of the problem.

cards.question: Which three factors must a manager consider when choosing a countermeasure?
options: Popularity, brand and age of the tool, as chosen by the vendor
Likelihood, impact and risk tolerance of the company
Security-effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and operational impact
Preventative, detective and corrective
options_why: These do not show if the tool fits the risk.
These are used to measure a risk, not to choose a countermeasure.
These are types of controls, not factors for choosing one.
cards.answer: Security-effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and operational impact
cards.explanation: A good measure protects against the real risk, is worth its price and does not block the work.

cards.question: Thefts cost $18,000 a year (ALE without protection). An anti-theft system costs $5,000 a year and brings the ALE down to $6,000. Is it worth its price?
options: No: 6,000 + 5,000 = $11,000, which is more than the $6,000 left
Yes: the system saves the whole $18,000
No: the cost of $5,000 a year is too high
options_why: You must compare with the ALE without the system, which is $18,000.
The loss is not zero. There is still $6,000 of ALE, and the system has a cost.
The cost must be compared with the loss. $5,000 is small next to $18,000.
cards.explanation: The total with the system is smaller than the ALE without it. The system saves $7,000 a year.

cards.question: Which measure helps MOST against an availability risk, such as a long power failure?
options: Backups
Encrypting all files
A longer password rule
Training on keeping secrets
options_why: Encryption protects secrecy. It does not keep files available.
Passwords protect access. They do not bring files back.
This targets confidentiality, not availability.
cards.answer: Backups
cards.explanation: A backup lets you get your data back. It answers the availability risk.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Security-Effectiveness”. The manual says to use resources for backups, not encryption, against availability risks.

cards.question: A control costs $4,000 a year and brings the ALE down from $3,000 to $500. What is the BEST decision?
options: Buy it, because the ALE falls by $2,500
Buy it, because the ALE becomes almost zero after the purchase
Buy it now and check the cost next year
Do not buy it: $4,500 in total is more than $3,000
options_why: The fall in ALE is smaller than the yearly cost of the control.
A tiny ALE does not help if the control costs more than the loss it prevents.
Check the numbers first. This control costs more than it saves.
cards.answer: Do not buy it: $4,500 in total is more than $3,000
cards.explanation: 500 + 4,000 = $4,500, which is more than $3,000. The control costs more than it prevents.

cards.question: A ransomware attack costs $40,000 a year (ALE without protection). A backup system costs $10,000 a year and brings the ALE down to $2,000. How much does the company save each year?
options_why: This forgets to count the $10,000 cost of the system.
This forgets that $2,000 of ALE is still there.
This is the total with the system (2,000 + 10,000), not the saving.
cards.explanation: The total with the system is 2,000 + 10,000 = $12,000. The saving is 40,000 - 12,000 = $28,000.

cards.question: Fraud costs a shop $12,000 a year (ALE). A protection costs $3,000 a year and brings the ALE down to $4,000. How much does the shop save each year?
options_why: This forgets to count the $3,000 cost of the protection.
This forgets that $4,000 of ALE is still there.
This is the total with the protection (4,000 + 3,000), not the saving.
cards.explanation: The total with the protection is 4,000 + 3,000 = $7,000. The saving is 12,000 - 7,000 = $5,000.

cards.question: A very strong tool costs more than the loss it prevents. The security team loves it. What is the BEST decision?
options: Buy the tool because it is the most secure one on the market
Buy the tool and ask leaders for a bigger budget
Choose a cheaper measure that costs less than the loss
Remove the risk from the list
options_why: A measure must also be cost-effective.
This spends more than the loss it prevents.
The risk still exists, even if this tool is too expensive.
cards.answer: Choose a cheaper measure that costs less than the loss
cards.explanation: Cost-effectiveness is a primary consideration for security teams and for management.

cards.question: A company forces staff to use a very hard email encryption tool. What is MOST likely to happen?
options: The emails will be safe even if nobody uses the tool or learns how
Some employees will send sensitive emails without encryption
Employees will learn the tool fast without training
The cost of the tool will go down over time
options_why: A protection that nobody uses protects nothing.
A hard tool needs training and care.
Cost has nothing to do with how hard a tool is to use.
cards.answer: Some employees will send sensitive emails without encryption
cards.explanation: Poor usability pushes people to bypass the control. The risk goes up.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Operational Impact”.

cards.question: A team plans to encrypt all files. The top risk on the list is a long power failure at the data center. What should the manager do FIRST?
options: Encrypt the files first, then add backups later if the budget allows
Ask vendors for the cheapest encryption that they can offer
Hire more staff to watch the servers
Match the measure to the risk: this risk needs backups, not encryption
options_why: Encryption does not fix the top risk, so it should not come first.
Price comes after you know the measure fits the risk.
More staff do not fix a power failure.
cards.answer: Match the measure to the risk: this risk needs backups, not encryption
cards.explanation: The manual says to pick countermeasures that directly address the risk you found.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT part of the cost to count for a countermeasure?
options: The first cost to buy it and to set it up in the company
The yearly cost to run it
The yearly cost to maintain it
The price of a different tool that you did not buy
options_why: This is the first cost of a countermeasure.
The manual says to count running costs every year.
The manual says to count maintenance costs too.
cards.answer: The price of a different tool that you did not buy
cards.explanation: You count the first cost and the yearly costs of the measure you choose.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Cost-Effectiveness” (Note box).

cards.question: Which kind of analysis compares the cost of a countermeasure with the cost of a compromise?
options: A maturity model
A cost-benefit analysis
A control assessment
A threat model
options_why: A maturity model measures how strong a program is.
A control assessment checks that controls work.
A threat model finds possible attacks.
cards.answer: A cost-benefit analysis
cards.explanation: A cost-benefit analysis compares what the protection costs with what the problem would cost.

cards.question: What does ALE stand for, and what is it?
cards.answer: Annual loss expectancy. It is the money that you expect to lose in one year because of a risk.
cards.explanation: Think of a yearly bill for a risk.

cards.question: What is the rule for a cost-effective countermeasure?
cards.answer: ALE with the measure, plus its cost, must be less than the ALE without the measure.
cards.explanation: Add the cost, then compare.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Cost-Effectiveness”.

cards.question: What costs come with a countermeasure, apart from the purchase price?
cards.answer: The costs to run and maintain it, every year.
cards.explanation: A protection is paid for at the start, then again every year.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Cost-Effectiveness” (Note box).

cards.question: Why can a control that is hard to use make a risk bigger?
cards.answer: People bypass it or do not use it. The control exists on paper, but the danger stays.
cards.explanation: A control only works if people use it.

paragraphes: Your bike has a good helmet and new brakes. Six months later, a brake is soft, and you did not notice.
A protection installed one day is not good forever. You must check it again and again.
In security, this check is called a security control assessment, or SCA.

decouverte.comme: A mechanic looks at your brakes. Then the mechanic asks you how you ride. Then the mechanic really tries the brakes on a test ramp.
decouverte.enVrai: An assessment uses three methods. Examine: read the documents and look at the settings. Interview: talk with the people involved. Test: run the protection and compare what was planned with what really happens.

decouverte.question: An assessor wants to know if the firewall really blocks forbidden connections. Which method proves it best?
options: Read the security policy
Ask the administrator
Try to send a forbidden connection
decouverte.answer: Try to send a forbidden connection
decouverte.explanation: Reading and asking give you one version of the story. A test compares real behavior with expected behavior.

decouverte.texte: The assessor first asks for documents, such as policies and configuration files. This is examining. Then the assessor meets the managers to understand how things work. This is interviewing. Finally the assessor tries the protection to see if it works as written. This is testing.

cards.question: Official definition: the methods for assessing controls (SCA)
cards.answer: There are many different SCA methodologies, but they generally include some form of the following assessment methods: examine, interview, and test.
cards.explanation: There are many ways to assess controls, but most use three methods: examine, interview and test.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Control Assessments”. SCA means security control assessment.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official one about “the assessment methods”?
options: There are many different SCA methodologies, but they generally include some form of the following assessment methods: examine, interview, and report.
There are many different SCA methodologies, but they generally include some form of the following assessment methods: observe, interview, and test.
There are many different SCA methodologies, but they generally include some form of the following assessment methods: examine, interview, and test.
There are many different SCA methodologies, but they always include every one of the following assessment methods: examine, interview, and test.
options_why: Report is not a method. The third method is test.
The first method is called examine.
The real sentence says generally include some form of. It does not say always and every one.
cards.answer: There are many different SCA methodologies, but they generally include some form of the following assessment methods: examine, interview, and test.
cards.explanation: Think of the mechanic: it looks, it asks, it tries.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about “the assessment methods” from memory.
cards.answer: There are many different SCA methodologies, but they generally include some form of the following assessment methods: examine, interview, and test.
cards.explanation: Think of the mechanic: it looks, it asks, it tries.

cards.question: Official definition: the forms of an “SCA”
cards.answer: SCAs may take the form of self-assessments or external assessments conducted by third parties.
cards.explanation: An SCA is done by the company itself or by an outside third party.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Control Assessments”. SCA means security control assessment.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about “the forms of an SCA” from memory.
cards.answer: SCAs may take the form of self-assessments or external assessments conducted by third parties.
cards.explanation: Self-assessment, or external assessment by third parties.

cards.question: Official definition: the “examine” method
cards.answer: Examine: This method is "the process of reviewing, inspecting, observing, studying, or analyzing one or more assessment objects (i.e., specifications, mechanisms, or activities)."
cards.explanation: To examine is to read and look at things: documents, settings and activities.
cards.explanation_more: Source: NIST 800-53A, quoted by the (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Control Assessments”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “examine” from memory.
cards.answer: Examine: This method is "the process of reviewing, inspecting, observing, studying, or analyzing one or more assessment objects (i.e., specifications, mechanisms, or activities)."
cards.explanation: Verbs of looking, on assessment objects: specifications, mechanisms and activities.

cards.question: Official definition: the “interview” method
cards.answer: Interview: This method is "the process of holding discussions with individuals or groups of individuals within an organization to once again, facilitate assessor understanding, achieve clarification, or obtain evidence."
cards.explanation: To interview is to talk with people in the company, to understand how the controls work.
cards.explanation_more: Source: NIST 800-53A, quoted by the (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Control Assessments”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “interview” from memory.
cards.answer: Interview: This method is "the process of holding discussions with individuals or groups of individuals within an organization to once again, facilitate assessor understanding, achieve clarification, or obtain evidence."
cards.explanation: Hold discussions with individuals or groups, to understand and to get evidence.

cards.question: Official definition: the “test” method
cards.answer: Test: This method is "the process of exercising one or more assessment objects (i.e., activities or mechanisms) under specified conditions to compare actual with expected behavior."
cards.explanation: To test is to make the protection work, and to compare what really happens with what was expected.
cards.explanation_more: Source: NIST 800-53A, quoted by the (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Control Assessments”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “test” from memory.
cards.answer: Test: This method is "the process of exercising one or more assessment objects (i.e., activities or mechanisms) under specified conditions to compare actual with expected behavior."
cards.explanation: Make it work, under set conditions, to compare real and expected behavior.

cards.question: An assessor reads the written security policies of a company. Which method is this?
options: Examine
Interview
Test
Self-assessment
options_why: Interviewing means talking with people.
Testing means making the protection work.
This is a form of assessment, not a method.
cards.answer: Examine
cards.explanation: Reading documents is examining.

cards.question: An assessor compares the real behavior of a protection with its expected behavior. Which method is this?
options: Examine
Test
Interview
Self-assessment
options_why: Examining means reading and looking, not making the protection work.
Interviewing means talking with people.
Self-assessment is a form of assessment, not a method.
cards.answer: Test
cards.explanation: Comparing real behavior with expected behavior is the definition of a test.

cards.question: Which of these is a form of assessment, and NOT a method?
options: Self-assessment
Examine
Interview
Test
options_why: Examine is one of the three methods.
Interview is one of the three methods.
Test is one of the three methods.
cards.answer: Self-assessment
cards.explanation: An SCA can be a self-assessment or an external assessment. The methods are examine, interview and test.

cards.question: An assessor needs proof that a firewall blocks forbidden connections. Which method gives the BEST proof?
options: Examine: read the firewall policy
Interview: ask the administrator how the firewall works
Examine: read the guide of the vendor
Test: send a forbidden connection and watch
options_why: A policy shows what should happen, not what does happen.
The administrator may be wrong or may not remember.
A guide describes the product, not this firewall in this company.
cards.answer: Test: send a forbidden connection and watch
cards.explanation: A test shows what the protection really does.

cards.question: An assessor starts a new assessment. Which method does the assessor often use FIRST?
options: Test: attack the protection at once, before reading anything
Interview: meet every employee
Examine: ask for the documents and the evidence
Report: write the final findings
options_why: Testing is better after you understand the system.
Interviews come after reading the evidence, to clarify.
A report comes at the end.
cards.answer: Examine: ask for the documents and the evidence
cards.explanation: Assessors often begin by asking for a list of evidence, such as policies and configuration files.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Control Assessments”.

cards.question: Which action gives the MOST proof that a nightly backup works?
options: Read the written backup procedure from start to end
Ask the administrator if it works
Restore a file from the backup and check it
Look at a log that says the backup is done
options_why: A procedure shows the plan. It does not prove that the backup works.
This gives an opinion, not proof.
A log says that something ran. It does not prove the data can be restored.
cards.answer: Restore a file from the backup and check it
cards.explanation: A restore is a test. It compares what really happens with what was expected.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three assessment methods?
options: Examine
Interview
Test
Report
options_why: Examine is one of the methods.
Interview is one of the methods.
Test is one of the methods.
cards.answer: Report
cards.explanation: The three methods are examine, interview and test. Reporting is what happens afterwards.

cards.question: Who can carry out a security control assessment?
options: The company itself, or an outside third party
Only government regulators who check the company
Only the vendor of the tool that is used in the company
Only the staff who run the controls
options_why: Regulators can assess, but they are not the only ones.
The vendor is not the only possible assessor.
Staff can do a self-assessment, but outsiders can assess too.
cards.answer: The company itself, or an outside third party
cards.explanation: An SCA can be a self-assessment or an external assessment by third parties.

cards.question: An assessor only reads the access policy of a company and says that controls are fine. What is the BEST criticism?
options: The policy should be shorter and easier to read for staff
Reading shows what is written, but a test shows if it works
Assessors must never read policies
Only interviews matter in an assessment
options_why: Length is not the problem.
Reading is a normal first step.
Interviews give opinions. Tests give proof.
cards.answer: Reading shows what is written, but a test shows if it works
cards.explanation: Paper does not prove that a protection works.

cards.question: An assessor meets key stakeholders to learn how controls work in practice. Which method is this?
options: Examine
Interview
Test
External assessment
options_why: Examining is reading and looking, without talking to people.
Testing means making the protection work.
This is a form of assessment, not a method.
cards.answer: Interview
cards.explanation: Holding discussions with individuals or groups is the interview method.

cards.question: How often should an organization assess its security controls?
options: Once, when the controls are installed and checked by the team
Only after a breach
Only when a law asks for it
Regularly, to make sure that they stay effective
options_why: Controls can wear out or drift out of adjustment.
The aim is to find problems before a breach.
The manual says you should do it in all cases, even when no law asks.
cards.answer: Regularly, to make sure that they stay effective
cards.explanation: Regular checks show that controls stay effective.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Control Assessments”.

cards.question: What is a security control assessment (SCA)?
cards.answer: A check that security and privacy controls work and stay effective.
cards.explanation: Like a check-up for a bike.

cards.question: Why do we assess controls regularly, even if they worked well at the start?
cards.answer: Because controls can wear out or drift out of adjustment over time. Regular checks show that they stay effective.
cards.explanation: A brake can be good one day and soft six months later.

cards.question: What is the test method mostly for?
cards.answer: To confirm that controls are in place as documented and that they work as expected.
cards.explanation: It is the method that shows what a protection really does.

cards.question: Why can a document alone not prove that a control works?
cards.answer: A document shows what should happen. Only a test shows what really happens.
cards.explanation: A well-written policy can still be ignored.

paragraphes: You want to run faster. You write down your training days, your goals and your time over 100 meters.
Every month, you read your notebook. You see what is getting better and what is stuck. Without a notebook, you would not know if you are making progress.
A company does the same for security: it monitors, it reports and it improves.

decouverte.comme: A bike computer shows your speed and distance. It does not pedal for you, but it tells you if you are going well.
decouverte.enVrai: Monitoring and measuring means watching all the time whether controls work. Key performance indicators, or KPIs, are the numbers on the computer. Reports tell the leaders what was found.

decouverte.question: A security team does audits and measures controls, but sends the results to nobody. What are they good for?
options: Nothing: without a report, they change no decision
Protecting the company: the audit is enough
Showing that people work, even if nobody reads them
decouverte.answer: Nothing: without a report, they change no decision
decouverte.explanation: The manual says these activities are useless without a good reporting function. The second answer is tempting because doing the audit feels like enough.

decouverte.comme: In a game, you have a level: 1, 2, 3, 4. You know your level, and you know what is left to do to reach the next one.
decouverte.enVrai: Risk maturity modeling places the security of a company on a scale of levels. The company sees which behaviors to improve, instead of chasing every single weakness. The image stops here: a company measures again and again. A level is not yours forever.

decouverte.texte: A security manager prepares a report. It includes internal audits, done by the company itself, and external audits, done by third parties. It adds big changes in risk or in controls. It also reports suspected or confirmed data leaks.

cards.question: Official definition: “risk maturity modeling”
cards.answer: Risk maturity modeling is a process that allows an organization to assess the strength of its security program and create a plan for continuous improvement based on their results.
cards.explanation: Risk maturity modeling measures how strong a security program is. Then the company makes a plan to get better.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Continuous Improvement”. The manual covers maturity models again in chapter 8.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “risk maturity modeling”?
options: Risk maturity modeling is a process that allows an organization to assess the strength of its security program and create a plan for continuous improvement based on their results.
Risk maturity modeling is a process that allows an organization to assess the strength of its security program and create a plan to buy new tools based on their results.
Risk maturity modeling is a process that allows an organization to assess the strength of its security program and measure the cost of a breach based on their results.
Risk maturity modeling is a process that allows an organization to assess the strength of its security staff and create a plan for continuous improvement based on their results.
options_why: The plan is for continuous improvement. It is not only for buying tools.
A maturity model leads to a plan for improvement. It does not measure the cost of a breach.
It assesses the security program, not the staff.
cards.answer: Risk maturity modeling is a process that allows an organization to assess the strength of its security program and create a plan for continuous improvement based on their results.
cards.explanation: Think of levels in a game: you measure your level, then you plan the next one.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “risk maturity modeling” from memory.
cards.answer: Risk maturity modeling is a process that allows an organization to assess the strength of its security program and create a plan for continuous improvement based on their results.
cards.explanation: Think of levels in a game: you measure your level, then you plan the next one.

cards.question: Official definition: watching and measuring controls (“monitoring”)
cards.answer: In addition to conducting periodic (e.g., annual or quarterly) security and privacy control assessments, you should actively and intentionally monitor your controls to measure their effectiveness and assess the health of your overall security program.
cards.explanation: On top of the regular assessments, you also watch your controls all the time, on purpose.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Monitoring and Measurement”.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about “monitoring controls” from memory.
cards.answer: In addition to conducting periodic (e.g., annual or quarterly) security and privacy control assessments, you should actively and intentionally monitor your controls to measure their effectiveness and assess the health of your overall security program.
cards.explanation: Watch on purpose, measure effectiveness, and judge the health of the program.

cards.question: Official definition: “KPIs”
cards.answer: Depending on your organization's needs, you should develop a set of key performance indicators (KPIs) that allow you to quantify and measure the long-term performance of your controls.
cards.explanation: KPIs are numbers that show how well your controls perform over a long time.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Monitoring and Measurement”. KPI means key performance indicator.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about “KPIs” from memory.
cards.answer: Depending on your organization's needs, you should develop a set of key performance indicators (KPIs) that allow you to quantify and measure the long-term performance of your controls.
cards.explanation: The full name, what they allow, and the time frame: the long term.

cards.question: Official definition: why “reporting” matters
cards.answer: Conducting SCAs and other monitoring and measurement activities is useless without a well-managed reporting function.
cards.explanation: Without a report, nobody knows the results. The work is pointless.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Reporting”.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about “why reporting matters” from memory.
cards.answer: Conducting SCAs and other monitoring and measurement activities is useless without a well-managed reporting function.
cards.explanation: Monitoring and measurement are useless without a well-managed reporting function.

cards.question: What does a KPI show?
options: The list of all the known threats of the company
The value of every asset
The performance of controls, measured over time
The price of the insurance policy
options_why: The list of threats is made when risks are identified.
Asset value is worked out during risk analysis.
A price is a cost, not a measure of performance.
cards.answer: The performance of controls, measured over time
cards.explanation: A KPI is a number that shows whether a control does its job, month after month.

cards.question: A company wants to know where its security program stands and to plan its progress. Which tool does it use?
options: Cyber insurance
A compensating control
A risk maturity model
A firewall
options_why: Insurance moves a loss. It does not measure a program.
A compensating control replaces a missing control. It measures nothing.
A firewall is a technical control. It does not measure a program.
cards.answer: A risk maturity model
cards.explanation: A maturity model places the program on a scale, then shows what to improve.

cards.question: Every week, a manager looks at numbers that show how the controls behave. Which activity is this?
options: Continuous monitoring
A periodic assessment
Risk transfer
Risk avoidance
options_why: A periodic assessment takes place on fixed dates, such as every year.
Nothing is moved to a third party.
No activity is stopped.
cards.answer: Continuous monitoring
cards.explanation: Monitoring watches all the time. Assessments take place at set times.

cards.question: A team runs audits and measures controls all year, but it sends the results to nobody. What is the BEST advice?
options: Stop running audits to save money and time for the team
Keep the results private to avoid worry among the staff
Run even more audits next year
Create a reporting process so that leaders see the results
options_why: The audits are useful. The problem is that nobody sees them.
Leaders need the results to decide.
More results that nobody reads do not help.
cards.answer: Create a reporting process so that leaders see the results
cards.explanation: The manual says that assessments are useless without a well-managed reporting function.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT on the manual's list of things to report?
options: Suspected security breaches
Every small update on one employee's computer
Significant changes to security controls
External audits
options_why: This is on the list, together with confirmed breaches.
This is on the list.
This is on the list, together with internal audits.
cards.answer: Every small update on one employee's computer
cards.explanation: The manual asks for reports on audits, big changes in risk or in controls, and suspected or confirmed breaches.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Reporting”.

cards.question: A data leak is only suspected, not confirmed. Which statement is MOST correct?
options: It should be reported, because suspected breaches count too
It should wait until the team is 100 percent sure
It should be reported only if a newspaper writes about it
It does not need a report, because only proven leaks count
options_why: Waiting for certainty delays the reaction.
The press is not the condition. Reporting is an internal duty.
The manual says suspected or confirmed breaches.
cards.answer: It should be reported, because suspected breaches count too
cards.explanation: It is better to warn early than too late.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Reporting”.

cards.question: A company buys new security tools every month and never checks if they help. What is the BEST way to improve?
options: Buy even more tools to cover every possible gap in security
Stop all spending on security until the next year starts
Measure the results with KPIs and improve the return on investment
Let each employee choose a tool that seems useful
options_why: More tools without measuring can waste money.
This would leave risks open.
Choices without a plan add confusion.
cards.answer: Measure the results with KPIs and improve the return on investment
cards.explanation: A CISSP should keep improving the return on investment of tools, controls and processes.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Continuous Improvement”.

cards.question: Which measure would be LEAST useful as a KPI for controls?
options: The number of accounts with a weak password
The number of people who work in the company
The average time to install security updates
The share of staff who passed a trick email test
options_why: This shows how well a password control works.
This shows how well the update process works.
This shows how well awareness training works.
cards.answer: The number of people who work in the company
cards.explanation: A KPI should say something about how a control performs. The size of the company does not.
cards.explanation_more: The example KPIs are teaching ideas (outside the manual).

cards.question: Why does the manual say that monitoring and assessments are useless without reporting?
options: Reports make audits cheaper
Reports are needed to pass the CISSP exam
Reports make the controls stronger by themselves
Leaders cannot act on results that they never see
options_why: Reports do not change the cost of audits.
The reason is about the company, not the exam.
Controls do not change just because a report exists.
cards.answer: Leaders cannot act on results that they never see
cards.explanation: A result that nobody reads changes no decision.

cards.question: Which statement about continuous improvement is NOT correct?
options: A CISSP should work to improve the return on investment
There is a fine line between not secure enough and too many tools
A CISSP should improve the efficiency of the security program
More security tools always mean better security
options_why: The manual says so.
The manual says so.
The manual says so.
cards.answer: More security tools always mean better security
cards.explanation: Too many tools and processes can be a problem, as well as too few.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Continuous Improvement”.

cards.question: A company has found its level on a risk maturity model. What does it do next?
options: It stops measuring
It makes a plan to improve
It buys cyber insurance
It removes controls at the lower levels
options_why: A maturity model is used again and again.
Insurance is a different treatment.
Lower levels show what to improve, not what to remove.
cards.answer: It makes a plan to improve
cards.explanation: The model shows the level and what to improve. The next step is the plan.

cards.question: What should the security team report? Name two things.
cards.answer: For example: internal and external audits, big changes in risk or in controls, or suspected or confirmed breaches.
cards.explanation: Five subjects in total.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Reporting”.

cards.question: What does KPI stand for?
cards.answer: Key performance indicator.
cards.explanation: A number on the computer of the bike.

cards.question: What does ROI mean for security?
cards.answer: Return on investment: how much protection each dollar brings. Not too little security, and not too many useless tools.
cards.explanation: It asks what the money spent brings back.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Continuous Improvement”.

cards.question: Why does a maturity model help more than fixing single gaps?
cards.answer: It shows the level of the whole program. The company can focus on the behaviors to improve, not on every single weakness.
cards.explanation: Think of the next level in a game.
